summary: Follow-up on the July 19th Aurora escalation: reviewed root cause (autoscaling edge case + KV cache eviction during model switch), short-term mitigations applied (sticky routing + fallback to smaller model), and longer-term reliability improvements (runbook updates, dedicated capacity suggestions, improved autoscaler safeguards). Agreed next steps: share postmortem, run dedicated repro, provide logs, and schedule runbook workshop.
transcript:
Meeting header: Date: 2027-07-21 14:00 PDT; Duration: ~58 mins; Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Ravi Patel (Redwood SE), Jordan Lee (CSM); Karen Li (Aurora Head of Platform), Daniel Moore (Aurora SRE), Priya Singh (Aurora Security), Luis Ortega (Product), Asha Patel (Ops)

[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone thanks for taking the time, I'll kick us off. This is the postmortem follow up for the July 19th outage you escalated, we want to make sure we're aligned on root cause and next steps. Uh, quick roll call?
[00:10] Karen Li: Hi Karen here, Daniel, Priya, Luis and Asha are on. Thanks Maya.
[00:15] Daniel Moore: Daniel here.
[00:20] Ravi Patel: Ravi from Redwood. I'll run through the technical findings.
[00:25] Jordan Lee: Jordan from CS. Noted.
[01:05] Maya Chen: Quick summary — what we saw was a spike in latency and a partial failure of requests between 02:13 and 02:42 UTC on July 19. Traffic pattern changed and our autoscaler triggered a model shard rebal, and during that window some requests routed to a variant without the KV cache warm which caused token regen and higher memory pressure leading to OOM on a subset of containers. We applied sticky routing and rolled back to the warm variant which stabilized things.
[01:40] Priya Singh: Quick clarification — when you say KV cache warm, you mean the prefix/KV cache in the runtime? We saw a lot of uncached token requests.
[01:48] Ravi Patel: Yeah that's right, the KV cache (sometimes transcribed in older notes as KV cash ha) — the worker keeps the attention KV cache in memory for serving fast continuation requests. The rebal led to transfers and some nodes hadn't populated the cache so cold starts were heavy.
[02:10] Karen Li: From our side we also had a sudden batch job that kicked off at 02:12 which increased sequence lengths. So two factors combined.
[02:25] Maya Chen: Right, combined load spike + autoscaler behavior. Our postmortem draft lists root causes: 1) autoscaler thresholds too aggressive for your tail distribution, 2) model-variant fallback policy didn't prefer warm caches, 3) runbook lacked exact rollback steps for that particular failure mode.
[02:45] Luis Ortega: Can you explain the model variant fallback? We thought Redwood would always route to the same model unless capacity exhausted.
[02:55] Ravi Patel: Good question — we have policy layers. By default we try same model + same variant but when capacity is constrained we will route to compatible variant to keep latency. In this case a variant without the warmed KV cache was available and chosen due to a sequencing of scale events. There's also a small bug in the routing priority logic that put cost-tier above cache-warmth in certain edge cases — that's in the repro.
[03:30] Daniel Moore: Was this on our dedicated pool or hosted? I remember we were on a mix since we spun up temporary dedicated during the PoC.
[03:38] Maya Chen: You were on Redwood Dedicated for your prod environment, but during the spike some canary traffic spilled into a nearby shared pool due to an autoscale burst config. So the mix is what created the variant mismatch.
[03:55] Asha Patel: That "shared pool" — is that the hosted cluster? 
[04:00] Ravi Patel: Yeah that's Redwood's hosted pool. There's an option to enforce strict isolation to avoid spillover; we'll note that as a config recommendation.
[04:20] Priya Singh: Security question — were any logs or persisted data exposed during this? We need to confirm there was no leak.
[04:26] Jordan Lee: Short answer: no data exfil. The affected requests timed out or returned elevated latencies but payloads were not persisted to other tenants. We'll attach audit logs.
[04:40] Priya Singh: Please share the audit log slice for that time window. Also any KMS key rotation events?
[04:48] Ravi Patel: No KMS rotations that window. We will export the audit logs and KMS events for 02:00-03:00 UTC.
[05:10] Maya Chen: Ok moving into mitigations: short-term we applied sticky routing to prefer warm cache nodes, increased autoscaler cooldowns, and forced a rollback to the warmed variant. Medium-term we've proposed config changes: stricter pool isolation (no spill to hosted), stricter fallback prioritization for warmed caches, and SLO alert tuning for tail latencies. Long-term: we plan runtime improvements — more graceful cache handoff, and autoscaler heuristic updates to use sequence-length-aware metrics.
[06:05] Karen Li: Can you give the timeline for those fixes? We need dates for our internal postmortem.
[06:12] Maya Chen: Sure. Short-term mitigations were applied same day (7/19). We'll deliver a postmortem doc with timelines by 7/23. Medium-term config changes we can propose by 7/25 and can apply to your dedicated pool after your sign-off. Runtime changes will need engineering cycles — target Q3 milestone for initial autoscaler heuristics and cache handoff improvements.
[06:40] Daniel Moore: For the repro, are you able to reproduce locally or do you need our production traces?
[06:48] Ravi Patel: We started a repro in our staging using a synthetic mix: long-seq batch at T0 + burst traffic. We can reproduce on a dedicated 4-GPU pool (r-dedicated-4gpu). To fully match your environment we need the production trace spans and the exact sequence-length histogram. If you can share, we'll run a more faithful repro and attach perf profiles, KV-cache traces, and kernel OOM logs.
[07:20] Karen Li: We'll get that to you.
[07:25] Priya Singh: Also attach your SOC 2 artifact for the audit. We logged the incident in our compliance tracker.
[07:30] Jordan Lee: We'll attach SOC 2 and ISO attestations and our audit log export for that window.
[07:50] Luis Ortega: I have a question about model quantization and mingling. Did the variant difference include a quantized model or smaller context window?
[07:58] Ravi Patel: It was the same architecture and quantization; the main difference was cache warm state and slightly different kernel selection due to different sequence-length profile. So not a different model per se, more of a warmed vs cold runtime state.
[08:20] Maya Chen: There's also an important note in the draft: our routing policy ranked nodes by cost tier before cache warmness in some path; we will flip that priority for your account as a stop-gap (config flag: prefer_cache_warmth=true).
[08:38] Daniel Moore: Will that increase costs?
[08:42] Maya Chen: Minimal, maybe a small bump during peak but should dramatically reduce the tail latency which from cost-perspective often outweighs raw compute price due to customer-facing errors.
[08:55] Asha Patel: We want a quantitative estimate — can you model expected cost delta if we disable spillover and prefer warmed nodes?
[09:02] Ravi Patel: We'll run cost sims on your June traffic slice and share numbers. That'll be in the perf profile pack.
[09:18] Karen Li: On communication — we had a bit of confusion on alerts. Our SREs saw the spike and tried the failover but unclear if Redwood had an automated fallback. Can you describe how Redwood SLO alerts integrate and who gets paged?
[09:32] Jordan Lee: By default we emit token-level latency and per-route error alerts to your PagerDuty integration if configured. In your case PD was configured, but the alert thresholds were at 95th/99th not the tail you were seeing; we recommend adding a specific 99.9th alert for model-serving tails. We'll propose alert thresholds.
[10:05] Daniel Moore: Ok please propose.
[10:10] Maya Chen: Switching gears to runbook: we noticed the documented rollback steps were generic. We'll supply precise runbook steps for this failure mode: how to lock routing to warmed variants, how to scale down the autoscaler safely, and how to force model pinning. We'll also schedule a workshop to walk your oncall through the steps.
[11:00] Karen Li: Good. Would like that hands on.
[11:15] Ravi Patel: One subtlety — the autoscaler cooldowns we recommended are sequence-aware (we will use moving-window percentiles). That avoids thrashing during sudden long-seq jobs. This is an engineering change but we can backport a config-driven heuristic sooner.
[12:05] Priya Singh: For compliance we need to capture the timeline and the mitigation evidence for our audit. Can you include timestamps and the change diffs (config changes, who approved)?
[12:18] Jordan Lee: Yes we'll include change diffs. We'll also include the admin audit trail showing the sticky routing flag flip and the rollback event.
[13:00] Maya Chen: Are there other immediate concerns from Aurora?
[13:06] Karen Li: Two things — one, we want reassurance that tenant isolation is bulletproof if we enforce stricter pool isolation, and two, a timeline for when the runtime improvements land.
[13:20] Ravi Patel: For tenant isolation, stricter pool isolation reduces blast radius and is recommended for enterprise. For the runtime timeline: config changes can be in by next week; engineering timelines for heuristic/autoscaler updates target mid-late Q3. We'll put dates in the postmortem.
[14:00] Luis Ortega: Will you also run a controlled chaos test to exercise the autoscaler and failover?
[14:08] Maya Chen: Yes good idea — we can collaborate on a controlled load test and chaos exercise ahead of the runbook workshop.
[14:40] Daniel Moore: One more technical ask — can we get the kernel-level OOM logs and the device memory traces? That would help us correlate with our sidecar metrics.
[14:50] Ravi Patel: We'll attach the kernel logs, nvml traces, and the runtime memory snapshots for the impacted nodes.
[15:15] Karen Li: OK timeline recap pls?
[15:20] Maya Chen: Recap: Redwood to share full postmortem draft + artifact links by 7/23; Redwood SE to run repro on dedicated cluster and share perf profiles and KV-cache traces by 7/25; Aurora to share production trace spans + sequence histogram by 7/22; Jordan to schedule runbook workshop week of 7/28; attach SOC2 + audit logs by Redwood.
[15:45] Priya Singh: We'll expect the SOC2 docs and the audit logs, please encrypt the shared bundle with our public key.
[15:52] Jordan Lee: We'll use the S3 presign + KMS envelope method per your preference.
[16:20] Luis Ortega: Any competitor moves noted? We are also evaluating vendor lock concerns and Anthropic's managed endpoints were mentioned earlier — how does Redwood compare on strict isolation?
[16:30] Maya Chen: Redwood allows dedicated-only isolation with VPC egress controls and optional on-prem for air-gapped needs. We'll map a comparison doc against Anthropic and OpenAI for your security/compliance review.
[17:05] Daniel Moore: Ok that's helpful.
[17:20] Asha Patel: On a process note, can you inject a post-incident checklist into our Jira project automatically?
[17:27] Jordan Lee: Yes we can create a template and create the ticket if you grant the integration. We'll send instructions.
[17:50] Maya Chen: Quick note on monitoring: we'll propose adding a 99.9th tail metric, a KV-cache-miss rate metric, and a node-warmness gauge. Those should be part of the alerting pack.
[18:16] Karen Li: Sounds good.
[18:30] Ravi Patel: I'll also add a temporary mitigation: we can set prefer_cache_warmth=true for Aurora's account immediately; that'll limit spillovers and prefer warmed nodes. It's reversible.
[18:45] Daniel Moore: Please apply that and tell us when done.
[18:50] Maya Chen: We'll apply as soon as we get sign-off.
[19:15] Priya Singh: On the legal/compliance side, any SLA credits for the incident? Our procurement team asked.
[19:23] Maya Chen: We'll route that through our customer success/legal channel; it's tied to the Dedicated contract terms — Jordan will follow up with the credits review.
[19:48] Jordan Lee: Noted; I'll open a ticket and loop legal.
[20:05] Karen Li: Anything else?
[20:08] Maya Chen: If not, we can go to questions.
[20:14] Luis Ortega: No more.
[20:20] Maya Chen: Ok thanks everyone. We'll send the postmortem and artifacts by 7/23 and reconvene after you validate the repro.
[20:28] Daniel Moore: Thanks.
[20:30] meeting end (note: remaining ~37 minutes of the scheduled hour were used for doc review and side conversations; recording clipped)

Notes about transcript quality: automated transcription had a few mis-typed product names (Redwood Dedicaed -> Dedicated, KV cash -> KV cache), speaker overlap in a couple places.

Referenced artifacts/links: Postmortem draft (link to be shared), Perf profile pack (redwood://perf/aurora/7-19), Audit logs export (redwood-s3://aurora-audit/2027-07-19.gz), SOC2 attestation PDF (redwood-sec://soc2/2026-v2.pdf), Repro runbook draft (link to shared doc).

End of transcript.
